interpretations.rationale: Index 17: node 3, seed 35 step 22, applied_before=3, applying_before=3, entry_index=4, entry_term=2, one change, joint-entering, joint_now=true, reapplied_entry=false. Index 18: node 1, step 23, identical operands. Index 19: node 4, step 31, applied_before=0, applying_before=0, same entry, reapplied_entry=false - a node rebuilt from persisted state consuming its log from the beginning. Index 20: three rejections among 245 configuration changes, 446 restarts, 481 elections, 51 unapplied-change check points, stalled_states=0, violations=0. Two conclusions follow and one remains open. Refuted with a receipt: the harness did not hand a node an entry whose index was already covered by its applied index - for nodes 3 and 1 the batch began exactly at applied_before+1, and for the rebuilt node 4 at its first entry - so the earlier suggestion that the rejections were double applications or an off-by-one in the harness is excluded, and the same holds for the weaker reading that the rejections come from application lag, since all three nodes were current with their commit index when the Changer rejected. Remaining open: whether the log the node consumed in order legitimately contained a joint-entering change at index 4 while its own configuration was joint. The propose-time guard in stepLeader rewrites a joint change when the proposing leader's own configuration is joint or when it has an unapplied configuration change, so if a node's log contains two joint-entering changes with no leave entry between them, one of those rewrites did not happen and either the guard's premises did not hold at the proposer or the proposer was not the node that saw the joint state. That distinction is not decidable from these four indices, which is why the defect claim stays unresolved even though the artifact reading is now excluded: what the receipt supports is that a node applying its own committed log in order can be handed a change its Changer rejects, and that the target's only reaction is the contract's panic - an availability consequence, with no safety violation observed.
counterevidence: violations=0 in the same receipt: none of the four safety invariants failed alongside the three rejections, so the consequence remains availability rather than divergence.
All three rejections come from one seed and one log position (index 4, term 2), so this receipt documents one configuration history rather than a distribution.

Nodes 3 and 1 were current with their commit index and still rejected, which argues against the lag-based story that the original harness failure suggested, but it does not by itself show that the change should not have been in the log.
The harness still skips a node's whole apply step about one time in six, which can make a node's configuration lag the leader's even when its applied index equals its commit index.
limitations: The receipt does not print the entry types and terms at the indices before 4 for the rejecting node, nor whether a leave-joint entry exists anywhere in that node's log, so the provenance of the joint-enter change is not yet observable.
Targets exclude the current leader, so no rejection was observed at a leader and the guard's leader-side premise is inferred from source rather than observed here.
Only the first three occurrences emit operands while the counter counts all rejections.

knowledge.assertion: a node can be handed a joint-entering change while its own configuration is joint, with the propose-time guard bounding only what the leader appends given its own applied configuration
